name: Gareth Rahman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI firms or campaigns. Your answers are confidential. Tell me about an ordinary day at work.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth Rahman, fifty-eight, and I'm a junior accountant at Alder Accounts, mainly preparing small charities' accounts and tax returns. I like showing a trustee which grant can pay which bill; chasing a missing receipt after closing time wears me out. My partner Leena works in a shop, and our grown children have their own homes, so we plan bills on our two wages.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to this desk?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I changed jobs later in life and earned a bachelor's degree in accounting. I'm still learning the tax side and ask our senior to check my entries; I never use AI tools, because I need to understand each grant line myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team at Alder Accounts that a receipt sorter won't settle a charity trustee's question about restricted money. A person still has to explain why a grant cannot pay the wrong bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am junior here and still slow at some tax checks, though my pay is ordinary for the post. My partner and I have about three months of expenses saved; the wage is steady now, but retirement is close enough that I notice every month we don't add to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep preparing the small charities' accounts with the paper grant letters beside the ledger, and ask the senior to review my tax entries before filing. I'd put thirty from each month's pay into the household reserve while our two wages continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than frightened. A little sorting help is fine, but I cannot make three months of savings feel like a long runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What part of the day goes well?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like when a trustee understands which donation can pay the heating bill after I show the letter. A missing receipt at five o'clock wears me out, especially when somebody assumes the grant will cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Do you use AI on those files?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I never use AI tools. I finished a bachelor's degree in accounting when I changed careers, and I still learn better by following the grant letter line by line with the senior.

I'd ask for a **human review** before tax returns go out.
think: My **junior wage** is steady, but our reserve is only three months.
Retirement is near enough to make **small savings** matter.
do: Keep **charity accounts** tied to paper grant letters and senior review.
Save **thirty monthly** from wages while both jobs continue.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about our short reserve.
S0.quote: A person still has to explain why a grant cannot pay the wrong bill.
fieldNote: Gareth's **junior checking** and senior sign-off continue under a modest sorter; he has never used AI tools.
His ordinary wage and **three-month cushion** support current bills but leave little room for a late-career interruption.

steps.text: Keep charity grant letters beside accounts and seek senior tax sign-off
Save thirty monthly from wages while both jobs continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff representative to get a written count of paid junior hours when the firm buys the return writer. We should know whose wage carries the change, not just how many returns the return writer prints.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Most of my day is entering and checking figures, so this software could remove the work I am still learning. I am fifty-eight, and with only three months saved I would find a cut to my own paid week hard to absorb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask our staff representative to request a written rota and paid training rule from Alder's partners next month. In the first year of steady change, if Alder cuts my paid week below four days, I'd apply for posted junior payroll work at the few firms nearby, keep every paid Alder day still offered, and move only after a written wage covering our bills and a start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a day of pay, not only about the software itself. I know my checking has gaps, and I can't buy time with a large reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new return writer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if Alder gives me paid supervised time with old charity files and the senior checks my errors. If it wants unpaid home practice, I'll stay with the approved ledger and ask the representative to record that refusal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no payroll post is advertised?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid Alder days that remain and ask the partners about the next month's rota. A nearby firm is only a possibility until it posts a funded job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the charity clients that full AGI in 2028 can prepare and check our accounts as well as people. Robots for hands-on work arrive about 2031, but they do not give my desk job extra years. I'd ask the partners for written notice if the junior desk is cut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect Alder to remove the junior tax desk, including mine, soon after 2028. My partner's shop wage and our three-month reserve would keep some bills paid, but they would not replace my income until retirement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the monthly sports subscription and put its sixty into emergency cash now. In the first year after 2028, if Alder ends my post, I'd apply for posted paid payroll-assistant work at the local college, keeping any paid Alder closing files only while the firm offers them until a written bill-covering wage and start date are confirmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because I expect my own wage to go before I have enough saved. I can cancel the sports club's sixty-a-month fee; I cannot cancel the loss of my accounting wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the college payroll desk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I used to handle staff timesheets at a shop, and the college pays people every month. AGI could do that thinking work too, so I would treat it as a possible paid opening, not a safe career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner tonight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my partner Leena that I want to stop the sports subscription while both of us still earn. I would show her the sixty going to the reserve, not claim the children should support us.

I'd seek **written notice** if junior posts close.

do: Cancel the **sports subscription** and save sixty monthly from wages.

fieldNote: His **three-month reserve** makes an expected 2028 loss of junior pay a near-term household problem.

steps.text: Cancel sports subscription and save sixty monthly from wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff group five years is time to demand a proper notice period, not a reason to wait quietly. Full AGI reaches our accounting desk in 2031; robots for physical work follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty-three I might still need wages, and I will not guess what retirement income will be. The junior work could go even if the charity clients still need someone to answer for a filing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff representative this year for a written notice and paid-hours plan and get an actual retirement-income statement before changing jobs. In the first year after 2031, if Alder closes my post, I'd apply for a posted college payroll vacancy with written bill-covering wage and start date, keeping paid closing work only while offered; if no paid vacancy opens, I'd continue searching without spending our reserve on an unposted course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed at the chance of a gap so close to retirement. Five years lets me ask questions, but it does not create another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the college asks for a certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a payroll module only if a real paid vacancy requires it and the college funds its fee and paid study time. If it doesn't, I won't pay for a certificate out of three months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stop work at sixty-three?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if the written income statement and our actual bills support that choice. I won't ask our grown children to fill a gap in my retirement money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to get the household numbers on one page. Full AGI reaches my accounts desk in 2036, and robots for hands-on work follow around 2039; my job does not wait for the robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be sixty-eight by then. I might have stopped work on a planned date, but I cannot claim that without seeing a written retirement-income figure and our bills; three months saved now is not a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a written retirement-income estimate next year and compare it with our actual bills each autumn while I keep paid Alder accounts work. In the first year after 2036, if that verified income covers essentials, I'd stay within our budget; if I still need wages and Alder's desk ends, I'd apply for posted paid college payroll with a written bill-covering wage and start date, taking any paid Alder closing files only while offered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy because I have time to check the figures, but no confirmed retirement income yet. I would not call a distant date a household plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you set a retirement date now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. The retirement estimate has to cover our heating bill before I put a date on the calendar. I want the written figures, actual bills and a conversation with Leena before making that promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the college posts nothing in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take any paid Alder files still offered and check other posted jobs nearby. If no wages are available, we'd use the reserve for essentials while continuing to search, not pretend an interview paid the bills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because a junior desk can disappear before I know what income retirement will bring. Written notice, paid closing work and a genuine posted payroll job with pay and a start would help more than an unfunded course.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how a charity explains a wrong grant charge to the donor. A machine can enter the number, but somebody still has to own the mistake in writing.

headlineQuote: A machine can enter the number, but somebody still has to own the mistake in writing.
portrait: Gareth, **fifty-eight**, is a junior charity accountant who likes explaining grant rules and dislikes missing receipts.
He has a **bachelor's degree**, is still learning tax checks and never uses AI tools.
Typical pay, **three months saved** and some nearby firms leave little room for a wage interruption.
He uses a **staff representative** to ask for written hours and notice while he checks actual retirement figures.
AGI could end his **junior desk** before he can replace its wage.
biggestWorry: He fears **AGI by 2028** will end his junior wage before retirement income is known.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice**, paid work while offered and a posted payroll vacancy with real terms.
